title: Radiation Physics for Radiography
description: Atomic structure and radioactivity, production of X-rays, interaction of radiation with matter, and radiation quantities and units.

topics.title: Atomic Structure and Radioactivity
topics.summary: Nuclear structure, types of radioactive decay, half-life and radionuclides in medicine.

notes.b: Unstable nuclei decay to more stable forms, emitting radiation. Alpha particles (2 protons + 2 neutrons, a helium nucleus) are heavy, highly ionising and stopped by paper or skin. Beta-minus particles are electrons emitted when a neutron converts to a proton; beta-plus (positrons) are emitted when a proton converts to a neutron and annihilate with electrons to give two 511 keV photons (the basis of PET). Gamma rays are high-energy photons from the nucleus, penetrating and stopped by lead or concrete. Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
k: Alpha: helium nucleus, stopped by paper

notes.b: Activity is the number of disintegrations per second, measured in becquerels (Bq; 1 Bq = 1 decay/s; old unit curie). Physical half-life is the time for activity to halve: after n half-lives, activity = initial × (½)ⁿ. Effective half-life combines physical and biological half-lives: 1/Te = 1/Tp + 1/Tb. Technetium-99m (half-life 6 hours, pure gamma emitter at 140 keV) is the most widely used diagnostic radionuclide; iodine-131 treats thyroid disease; fluorine-18 (110 min) is used in FDG-PET.

topics.title: Production of X-rays and the X-ray Tube
topics.summary: X-ray tube components, bremsstrahlung and characteristic radiation, and exposure factors.

notes.b: X-rays were discovered by Wilhelm Röntgen in 1895. In the X-ray tube, a heated tungsten filament in the cathode releases electrons by thermionic emission; a high voltage (kilovoltage, kVp) accelerates them across a vacuum to strike the anode target (tungsten, high atomic number 74 and melting point ~3,400 °C). Over 99% of the electron energy becomes heat and less than 1% becomes X-rays, so rotating anodes and oil cooling are used. The line-focus principle (angled anode) gives a small effective focal spot for sharp images while spreading heat over a larger actual area. The heel effect makes intensity lower on the anode side.
k: Tungsten target: high Z, high melting point
Heel effect: less intensity on anode side

notes.b: Bremsstrahlung ('braking') radiation forms most of the beam, producing a continuous spectrum up to the peak kilovoltage. Characteristic radiation occurs when an incoming electron ejects an inner-shell (K-shell) electron and an outer electron fills the vacancy, emitting discrete energies. kVp controls beam energy (penetration and contrast); mA × exposure time (mAs) controls the quantity of X-rays and hence image density/noise. Filtration (aluminium) removes low-energy photons that would only add to skin dose ('beam hardening').

Characteristic: discrete lines from shell transitions

topics.title: Interaction of Radiation with Matter
topics.summary: Photoelectric effect, Compton scattering, attenuation and image contrast.

notes.b: In the diagnostic energy range the main interactions are the photoelectric effect and Compton scattering. In the photoelectric effect a photon is completely absorbed by an inner-shell electron; its probability is roughly proportional to Z³/E³, so it dominates at low energies and in high-Z materials (bone, iodine and barium contrast, lead). It produces image contrast and increases patient dose. In Compton scattering a photon interacts with an outer electron, losing part of its energy and changing direction; it depends on electron density, dominates at higher energies in soft tissue, degrades image quality (fog) and is the main source of occupational scatter dose. Pair production requires energies above 1.022 MeV (radiotherapy range).

Attenuation is the reduction of beam intensity by absorption and scatter: I = I₀e^(−μx), where μ is the linear attenuation coefficient. The half-value layer (HVL) is the thickness of material that halves beam intensity. Contrast on a radiograph arises from differences in attenuation: bone (high Z and density) appears white (radio-opaque), air appears black (radiolucent), soft tissue and fat are grey. Lower kVp increases contrast (more photoelectric absorption). Anti-scatter grids and collimation reduce scatter reaching the image receptor.

topics.title: Radiation Quantities, Units and Biological Effects
topics.summary: Absorbed, equivalent and effective dose, and deterministic and stochastic effects.

notes.b: Absorbed dose is energy deposited per unit mass, measured in gray (Gy = J/kg). Equivalent dose = absorbed dose × radiation weighting factor (1 for X-rays, gamma and beta; 20 for alpha), measured in sieverts (Sv). Effective dose sums equivalent doses to organs multiplied by tissue weighting factors and estimates overall stochastic risk (Sv). Typical effective doses: chest X-ray about 0.02 mSv; CT abdomen about 8–10 mSv; natural background about 2–3 mSv per year.
k: Chest X-ray ≈ 0.02 mSv; CT abdomen ≈ 10 mSv

notes.b: Ionising radiation damages DNA directly or indirectly via free radicals from water (indirect action predominates for X-rays). Deterministic (tissue) effects have a threshold and their severity increases with dose — e.g. skin erythema, cataract, hair loss, sterility, acute radiation syndrome. Stochastic effects (cancer, heritable effects) have no threshold; the probability, not severity, increases with dose. The law of Bergonié and Tribondeau states that cells are more radiosensitive when they divide rapidly and are less differentiated — lymphocytes, bone marrow, gonads and the fetus are highly sensitive; nerve and muscle are resistant.

topics.title: Image Receptors and Digital Imaging Basics
topics.summary: Film–screen, computed and digital radiography, and image quality parameters.

notes.b: Traditional film–screen systems use intensifying screens containing phosphors (e.g. rare-earth gadolinium oxysulphide) that convert X-rays to light to expose film, reducing patient dose. Computed radiography (CR) uses photostimulable phosphor plates (barium fluorohalide) that store the latent image and release light when scanned by a laser. Direct digital radiography (DR) uses flat-panel detectors: indirect (scintillator such as caesium iodide + photodiodes) or direct (amorphous selenium converts X-rays directly to charge). Images are stored and shared through PACS in DICOM format.
k: CR: photostimulable phosphor plate read by laser

notes.b: Key image-quality factors are contrast (difference in density between structures), spatial resolution (ability to show fine detail), noise (random variation, reduced by increasing mAs) and artefacts. Geometric unsharpness is reduced by a small focal spot, a short object–image distance and a long source–image distance. Magnification = SID/SOD. The inverse square law states that intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the source (doubling distance quarters intensity) — the basis of distance as radiation protection.
k: Small focal spot + short OID + long SID = sharper
